description: We are a team from Karachi, Pakistan, passionate about space and education. We are building an interactive game where students design, launch and run a complete space mission, balancing budget, mass, power and communications. Players learn how real engineering decisions shape the success of a mission, all through hands-on play.
summary:
MissionX is a browser-based educational game where players design, verify, launch and review a complete space mission. Players choose Moon Mapping, Sun Watch or Mars Orbiter, then build a spacecraft while balancing mass, budget, power, battery capacity, onboard storage and communications. After verification checks, a seeded launch scenario runs, and players get an explainable result and a downloadable mission report before redesigning.

MissionX addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning real mission trade-offs into playable decisions: a more capable instrument adds science value but also costs mass, power, data and money. Results explain why a mission succeeded or failed across the four mission segments: Launch, Space, Ground and User.

It matters because students rarely get to experiment with a whole mission from concept to operation. MissionX makes those connections visible and encourages iteration. NASA mission pages provide real-world context, while all numbers are authored educational values, not live NASA data.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS
MissionX turns spacecraft design into an interactive learning loop: Goal, Build, Verify, Launch, Result. Players pick one of three missions (Moon Mapping, Sun Watch with four small satellites, Mars Orbiter), build a spacecraft from 26 parts across eight categories, choose a fictional launcher and a synthetic orbit, and resolve verification checks before launch. A seeded simulation then produces a launch outcome and one operational event. A pure TypeScript engine calculates mass, budget, solar generation, battery use, data generation, onboard storage and downlink. Science credit depends on data that actually reaches Earth, so a powerful instrument can still fail if power, memory or communications are insufficient.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
MissionX helps beginners see that every design choice has consequences, that there is no single perfect answer, and that a result should be explained by evidence. Results separate mission outcome (success, partial, failed) from a weighted performance score and explain causes across the four real mission segments: Launch, Space, Ground and User. Players can compare saved attempts, redesign, and download a PDF report. We hope to make mission design approachable for students and educators. This is a design intention, not a measured learning outcome.

TOOLS
Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, Zustand, GSAP, Lenis, pdf-lib, Web Audio API, Bun and Vercel. An optional server-side AI mentor can give short advice, and local fallback advice works without it. No special hardware is needed, only a web browser.

CREATIVITY
Arrival reviews use PASS, WARNING, FAIL and NOT EVALUATED, so missing measurements are never shown as passed. Mission outcome and score are deliberately separate, so a high score cannot hide a missed requirement. The same rules power both a 3D mission headquarters and a simple flight-deck view, and launches are reproducible with a seed so players can investigate exactly why a mission changed.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
Accuracy versus approachability: all numbers are authored educational values, clearly labelled, with no claim of NASA validation or flight certification. We designed for beginners, with plain-language explanations, no account required, and a no-WebGL fallback and reduced-motion options. NASA mission pages and a NASA systems-engineering presentation guided the mission structure. MissionX is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.
